title: Next year's text
hook: choose what you'll study next: a book of Tanakh, a tractate, a code
tomorrow: why would the Talmud threaten people who study alone?

segments.voice: Yesterday, from strength to strength, and a finish that promises to come back. Never graduated. So if there's no finish line, where do you start next?

A stack of maybe-someday books on a nightstand, the top one with its bookmark stuck near the start. Choosing what to read next can stall a person for months. Avot de-Rabbi Natan tells of a grown man named Akiva who had never learned anything at all. One day, by a well, he sees a stone with a hollow worn into it. Who carved this, he asks. Water, they tell him. The water that falls on it, day after day.
screen: `MAYBE-SOMEDAY BOOKS.` → `A STONE BY THE WELL.` → `WHO CARVED THIS? WATER.`

segments.voice: Akiva thinks: if soft water can hollow hard stone, words of Torah can carve a place in my heart, which is only flesh and blood. So he goes with his young son, and the two of them sit down before a teacher of children. And what does a grown man read first? The alef-bet. Letters. Then, the story says, Torat Kohanim, the book of Leviticus, and on and on, until he had learned the whole Torah. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: a midrash says children once began the Torah not with Genesis but with Leviticus, the laws of offerings, because, it says, the pure should come and study what is pure. So what's next year's text? The tradition offers real choices. A book of Tanakh, read slowly. A tractate of Talmud. A code, like the laws Maimonides gathered. The choice matters less than the dripping. Pick the one you'll actually open, again and again, until it wears a place in you. Akiva chose the alef-bet, beside his son. Nobody would call it the hardest text. It was the right one.
screen: `IF WATER CAN CARVE STONE…` · `HE BEGINS WITH THE ALEF-BET.` · `CHILDREN BEGAN WITH LEVITICUS.` · `A BOOK, A TRACTATE, A CODE.` · then, large: `CHOOSE NEXT YEAR'S TEXT.`

segments.voice: Pick up one book near you, or open one on a screen: something you've meant to read. Hold it, look at it, and read its first line slowly. Then ask one question: is this the text I'd open again and again next year?
screen: `ONE BOOK IN YOUR HANDS.` · `THE FIRST LINE, SLOWLY.` · `AGAIN AND AGAIN?`

segments.voice: Next year's text: the one book you choose to study in the year ahead, a book of Tanakh, a tractate, a code, opened again and again like water on stone.
Something to keep: choose next year's text. Drip by drip, it wears a place in you. Until next time.

howItsDone: Jewish adults often choose a text to study for a season or a year: a book of the Tanakh, a tractate of Talmud, or a section of a code such as Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, alone, with a partner or in a class.

chat.meaning: Akiva began with letters, then Leviticus. The right text is one you'll open again and again, like water on stone.

Akiva.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah who began learning as a grown man

Avot de-Rabbi Natan.meaning: an early companion to Pirkei Avot, full of stories

Torat Kohanim.meaning: the teaching of the priests: an old name for Leviticus

midrash.meaning: a rabbinic reading of scripture, often through story

Tanakh.meaning: the Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets and Writings

sources.ref: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 6 (Akiva sees the stone hollowed by water; learns with his son before a children's teacher: the alef-bet, Torat Kohanim, until the whole Torah)
Vayikra Rabbah 7:3 (why young children begin with Torat Kohanim: let the pure come and occupy themselves with the pure)
